status: Draft from the mishnah and Kehati. Chapters 1-6 form a unit about damage caused by one's property or act.

principles.t: Four primary causes of injury (avot nezikin): the ox (shor), the pit (bor), the crop-destroying beast (mav'eh) and fire (hev'er). Each is in the Torah, and each has a feature the others lack.
What I am bound to guard, if I did not guard it, I have prepared its damage, even if only partly.
Damages are paid only for property that is not sacred, belongs to Jews, is owned, and is damaged outside the damager's own domain and the domain shared by both.
Damages are assessed in money before a court of experts on the evidence of free Jewish witnesses. Women are included.
A harmless animal (tam) pays half damages from its own body; an attested danger (mu'ad) pays full damages with the best of the land.

terms.def: The four basic categories of damage in the Torah: ox, pit, crop-destroying beast and fire.

locus.name: Bava Kamma
locus.why: Listed in 1:1; the tooth in 2:2, the pit in 5:5–5:7 and fire in 6:4–6:6.

terms.def: An animal not yet attested as a danger for a given damage; it can still do damage.

locus.name: Bava Kamma
locus.why: Defined in 1:4; how an ox stops being a tam in 2:4; half damages for a tam in 3:8, 4:1 and 5:1.

terms.more: Its owner pays half damages from the animal's own value.

terms.def: An animal or person whose way is to do damage, or an animal that has been warned (attested) to do it.

locus.name: Bava Kamma
locus.why: Defined in 1:4; the foot and tooth in 2:1–2:2; a person in 2:6; how an ox becomes a mu'ad in 2:4; a mu'ad for some damage only in 4:2.

terms.more: The one responsible pays full damages with the best of the land. A human being is always a mu'ad.

terms.term: with the best of the land
terms.def: The payment for full damages comes with the best of the land.
Using sacred property (hekdesh) for one's own benefit.
terms.more: It appears here only in passing: the laws of damages cover property that is not subject to me'ilah, that is, an ordinary person's property and not the Temple's.

terms.def: The one responsible for the damage: the owner of the ox, pit or fire that did the damage, or the person who did it.

locus.name: Bava Kamma
locus.why: Throughout the tractate; the domains in 1:2.

terms.more: He pays full damages with the best of the land, assessed in money before a court. There is no payment for damage in his own private domain.

terms.def: The one who suffered the damage: the owner of the damaged property, or the injured person.

locus.name: Bava Kamma
locus.why: Throughout the tractate; the domains in 1:2.

terms.more: He collects only for property that is not sacred, belongs to Jews and is owned.

terms.def: The ox: one of the four primary causes of injury. It is alive, and its way is to go out and do damage.

locus.name: Bava Kamma
locus.why: The foot in 2:1; the horn in 2:4–2:5; oxen that gore in chapter 4.

terms.more: The Gemara disputes what the mishnah's "ox" includes: Rav says damage by horn, tooth and foot; Shmuel says only the foot, damage by its walking. Goring with the horn is treated separately, in 2:4-2:5 and chapter 4.

terms.def: The pit: one of the four primary causes of injury. Unlike the ox and fire, its way is not to go out and do damage: the victim walks or falls into it.

locus.name: Bava Kamma
locus.why: The laws of the pit in 5:5–5:7.

terms.more: One who digs or opens a pit where he has no right to is liable for an animal that falls in and dies or is injured, but only if the pit is ten handbreadths deep for a death (a shallower one makes him liable for an injury only), and not for vessels or for a person.

terms.def: The crop-destroying beast, named from a word meaning to bulge out: one of the four primary causes of injury. Like the ox, its way is to go out and do damage.
terms.more: Shmuel takes it as the tooth: an animal eating what is fit for it, an attested danger (mu'ad) from the start. Rav takes it as a person who damages.

terms.def: Fire: something with no living spirit whose way is to go out and do damage. One of the four primary causes of injury.
terms.more: The one who kindles it must guard it, and pays for what it burns, wood, stones and earth included.

debates.title: What are the four primary causes of injury?
debates.a: The mishnah names the main kinds of damage in the Torah.
debates.b: It names only four kinds of property damage that are attested dangers from the start (foot, tooth, pit, fire).

debates.title: Do tame wild animals count as attested dangers?
debates.a: The wolf, lion, bear, leopard, panther and snake are attested dangers.
debates.b: Tame ones are not, but the snake always is. The halakha does not follow him.
